bill.title: To direct the Secretary of Defense to establish test and training corridors for small unmanned aircraft systems and associated capabilities, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

industries.rationale: The bill directs the Department of Defense to establish testing infrastructure specifically for military unmanned aircraft systems and associated capabilities.
Companies developing drone hardware, software, sensors, and autonomous systems would gain access to dedicated testing corridors for their technologies.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require the Secretary of Defense to create designated test and training corridors for small unmanned aircraft systems (drones). These corridors would provide areas where the military and potentially other entities could develop and test drone technologies and related capabilities. The bill does not specify the number, location, or detailed operational parameters of these corridors.

bill.title: Providing congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine and Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; The "Omnibus" Low NOX Regulation; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects emissions compliance obligations for manufacturers and operators of heavy-duty trucks, buses, and diesel-powered vehicles and equipment.
Vehicle and engine manufacturers would face different regulatory requirements depending on whether California's stricter emissions standards remain in effect or are preempted by federal rules.
Construction firms use off-road diesel equipment covered by the waiver, and the bill would affect compliance costs and equipment specifications for these machines.
Agricultural operations use off-road diesel engines and heavy-duty vehicles subject to the emissions standards that would be affected by revoking the waiver.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would cancel a waiver that allows California to enforce stricter emissions standards than federal rules for heavy-duty trucks, buses, and off-road diesel equipment starting with 2024 models. The waiver, granted by the Environmental Protection Agency under the Clean Air Act, permits California to set its own limits on nitrogen oxide pollution from these vehicles and engines. If passed, the resolution would restore federal preemption and prevent California from enforcing these particular state-level standards.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who drives. People living near a road, a plant or a port.

bill.title: No Taxpayer Funding for Abortion and Abortion Insurance Full Disclosure Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committees on the Judiciary, and Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts what health insurance plans may cover and how federal subsidies interact with abortion coverage in qualified health plans.
The bill prohibits federal health care facilities and federal employees from providing abortion services, affecting facilities that currently receive federal funds.
Organizations focused on reproductive health policy and abortion access or restrictions have a direct stake in the regulatory framework this bill establishes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make permanent the restrictions on federal funding for abortion services and health insurance coverage that includes abortion. Currently, these restrictions are renewed each year through appropriations bills; the bill would apply them across all federal programs and funds. It would also prohibit qualified health plans offered through insurance marketplaces from covering abortion. The bill includes exceptions for cases of rape, incest, or when the pregnant person's life is in danger.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys health insurance. Anyone who pays a medical bill.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters".

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of gas-fired instantaneous water heaters would be directly affected by the nullification of energy efficiency standards that govern their products.
The natural gas industry has a stake in standards that affect the efficiency and market viability of gas-fired appliances.
Gas utilities that supply fuel for these water heaters would be affected by standards that influence appliance efficiency and gas consumption.
Homebuilders and property developers install water heaters in new construction and would be affected by changes to appliance standards and costs.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would block a Department of Energy rule that set new energy efficiency standards for gas-fired tankless water heaters. The rule, finalized in December 2024, required these appliances to meet stricter energy conservation requirements. If passed, the resolution would nullify those standards and prevent them from taking effect.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys fuel or heats a home.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Walk-In Coolers and Walk-In Freezers".

industries.rationale: Grocery stores and restaurant chains operate walk-in coolers and freezers and would face different equipment compliance costs depending on whether the standards take effect.
Manufacturers of walk-in coolers, freezers, doors, and refrigeration systems would need to redesign products to meet the new standards or continue current designs if the rule is nullified.
Hotels and large food-service operations use walk-in refrigeration and would be subject to the equipment standards.
Food processing and cold-storage facilities use walk-in refrigeration equipment and would be affected by changes in equipment efficiency requirements.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would block a Department of Energy rule that set stricter energy efficiency standards for walk-in coolers and freezers used in commercial settings. The rule, finalized in December 2024, would have required walk-in refrigeration equipment to meet new energy consumption limits starting in 2027 and 2028. If passed, the resolution would nullify those standards and leave the existing, less stringent requirements in place.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act
bill.latestActionText: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 10.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates new litigation exposure for federal agencies, affecting federal and state government operations and budgets.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, increasing demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to detain individuals who are in the country without authorization and have been arrested for or charged with burglary, theft, larceny, or shoplifting. It would also allow state governments to sue the federal government for injunctive relief when federal immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing individuals from custody or not fulfilling visa or asylum processing requirements—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers working with controlled substances and affects the regulatory classification of fentanyl-related compounds.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect defense attorneys and prosecutors handling drug trafficking cases.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and makes it easier for registered researchers to conduct certain activities without additional permits.

plain.whoItTouches: People caught up in the criminal law, and victims of crime.

bill.title: SAVE Moms and Babies Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
subjects: Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly prohibits approval of new abortion drugs and imposes significant new regulatory restrictions on already-approved drugs in this category.
The bill creates new certification requirements for prescribing practitioners and mandates they have surgical intervention capability, changing practice obligations.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit the FDA from approving any new drugs intended to terminate pregnancy. For drugs already approved for this purpose, it would impose new restrictions: requiring in-person dispensing by a specially certified practitioner, prohibiting use after 70 days of gestation, and mandating that the practitioner be able to provide surgical intervention. The bill would also prevent practitioners from both prescribing and dispensing these medications.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who fills a prescription. Anyone who takes a medicine.

subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers face different emission and zero-emission vehicle requirements depending on whether California's waiver stands or is revoked.
Zero-emission vehicle mandates directly affect demand for gasoline and diesel fuel in California's large vehicle market.
Electric vehicle adoption rates influence demand for charging infrastructure and electricity from renewable sources.
The pace of electric vehicle deployment affects electricity demand and grid infrastructure investment needs.

Those regulations set stricter standards for vehicle emissions and require automakers to sell more zero-emission vehicles in California. If the resolution passes, California would lose the authority to enforce these stricter rules, reverting to federal emission standards.

Hotels and other hospitality businesses are major users of commercial water heating equipment and would be affected by changes in equipment efficiency standards and costs.
Restaurants and other retail establishments that rely on commercial water heating would face different equipment costs and energy expenses under the competing standards.
Hospitals and healthcare facilities use commercial water heating equipment and would be affected by changes in equipment efficiency requirements and operating costs.

The rule, finalized in October 2023, was designed to reduce energy consumption by commercial water heating equipment. If passed, the resolution would nullify these updated standards and leave the previous, less stringent requirements in place.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Management of Certain Hydrofluorocarbons and Substitutes Under the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020".
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of refrigeration equipment, air conditioning systems, and products using hydrofluorocarbons face direct regulatory obligations under the nullified rule.
The rule establishes recycling and reclamation standards for spent refrigerants, directly affecting waste management and recycling operations.
Electric utilities using refrigeration and cooling systems in power generation may be subject to the hydrofluorocarbon management requirements.
Building contractors and HVAC installers work with refrigeration systems and would be affected by standards governing hydrofluorocarbon handling and disposal.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify an Environmental Protection Agency rule published in October 2024 that manages hydrofluorocarbons, which are greenhouse gases used in refrigeration and other applications. The EPA rule created a program to reduce emissions and reclaim these substances, and set recycling standards for certain spent refrigerants. If this resolution passes, that rule would be canceled and would have no legal effect.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects regulatory obligations for trucking companies and heavy-duty vehicle operators subject to California emission standards.
The bill would change compliance requirements for manufacturers of heavy-duty trucks and engines sold in California.
Revoking zero-emission truck mandates would reduce market requirements for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean powertrain technology.
Changes to zero-emission vehicle requirements could affect electricity demand and infrastructure planning for fleet electrification.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would cancel waivers that allow California to enforce its own stricter emission standards for heavy-duty trucks and engines. Under the Clean Air Act, California can request permission to set its own vehicle pollution rules that are tougher than federal standards; this resolution would revoke several such waivers related to truck emissions, warranties, zero-emission airport shuttles, and advanced clean truck requirements. If passed, California would lose the authority to enforce these particular state-level vehicle pollution rules.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of commercial refrigeration equipment would no longer need to meet the stricter energy efficiency standards that were set to take effect in 2029.
Grocery stores, restaurants, and other food retailers that purchase and operate commercial refrigeration equipment would be affected by whether they must buy equipment meeting the new standards.
Hotels and restaurants use commercial refrigeration equipment and would be affected by the regulatory requirements for equipment they purchase.
Electric utilities would see different demand patterns depending on whether commercial refrigeration equipment must meet higher efficiency standards.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would cancel a Department of Energy rule that set stricter energy efficiency standards for commercial refrigerators, freezers, and similar equipment used by businesses. The rule, published in January 2025, would have required this equipment to meet new energy conservation standards by January 2029. If this resolution passes, those updated standards would be eliminated and the equipment would not need to comply with the new requirements.

bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of refrigeration, air conditioning, and cooling equipment would be directly affected by changes to HFC management and recycling requirements.
The rule establishes recycling standards for spent refrigerants, directly affecting waste management and recycling operations for these materials.
Electric utilities often use HFC-based cooling systems in power generation facilities and would be subject to the emission reduction program.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency rule that manages hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which are potent greenhouse gases used in refrigeration and air conditioning. The EPA rule, published in October 2024, sets up a program to reduce HFC emissions and establish recycling standards for spent refrigerants. If this resolution passes, that rule would be nullified and would have no legal effect.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
